draft.title: Oxygen uptake
card: Oxygen deficit
at the start of exercise, oxygen uptake rises more slowly than the body's demand. The gap is made up by energy systems that do not need oxygen.
Steady state
if the intensity stays fairly low and constant, oxygen uptake levels off and meets demand. Energy is then supplied mainly by the aerobic system.
EPOC
after exercise, oxygen uptake stays above resting level. This excess post-exercise oxygen consumption helps the body recover, for example by restoring fuel stores and removing by-products.
A very hard effort may never reach a steady state, because demand keeps rising faster than oxygen can be supplied.
draft.remember: Uptake lags at the start, levels off if the effort is steady, and stays raised after.

a.q: Why is there an oxygen deficit at the start of a jog?
opts: Oxygen uptake rises more slowly than the oxygen demand
The body has no oxygen available at the start
Oxygen uptake is higher than the oxygen demand
The aerobic system is not used at any point in the jog
a.why: Demand jumps as soon as the jog begins, but uptake takes time to climb. The gap is the deficit. It is wrong to say the body has no oxygen: uptake is rising, just not fast enough.
a.clue: Compare how fast demand and uptake each rise.

b.q: Priya cycles at a steady, easy pace for 20 minutes, then stops and rests. Her breathing stays faster than normal for several minutes. What does this show?
opts: EPOC, as oxygen uptake is still above resting level
Oxygen deficit, as uptake is lower than demand
Steady state, as uptake has levelled off during rest
Fatigue, as her oxygen uptake has fallen below resting
b.why: Raised oxygen uptake after exercise is EPOC, and it supports recovery. Steady state describes the constant effort during the ride, not the period after it.
b.clue: Look at when the raised breathing happens: during or after the ride.

a.best: Oxygen uptake rises more slowly than the oxygen demand

b.best: EPOC, as oxygen uptake is still above resting level

problems.detail: The steady-state line limits steady state to efforts that are 'fairly low'. In VCE PE, steady state can be reached at any constant submaximal intensity, including moderate to fairly high efforts below the lactate inflection point. Students may wrongly think moderate or hard steady efforts cannot reach steady state.

'Demand keeps rising faster than oxygen can be supplied' is misleading for a constant very hard effort. The demand does not keep rising. It is simply above what the aerobic system can supply, so uptake cannot match it.

check.summary: Both questions are sound and have a single clear answer. Two card lines need fixing: steady state is not limited to 'fairly low' intensity, and a very hard effort lacks a steady state because demand is above what can be supplied, not because demand keeps rising.
